Secret Society Infiltration Map

Where lodges, religious orders, policy clubs, international bodies and covert networks reached inside governments — 193 states scored, and the cases a court, inquiry or government confirmed
Map rundown−
Nobody keeps a register of which officials belong to which society, and most of these organisations exist so that no such register can be compiled. Membership lists surface when a police raid finds one, as at Licio Gelli's villa in 1981; when a parliament orders one handed over, as Britain's did for Masonic police officers in 1999; or when a government falls and the next one opens the files, as in Turkey after 2016.

So this map does not claim to count infiltration. It carries layers that can each be checked, and keeps them apart.

The first is a 193-country score. Half of it is the documented record below, weighted by how far each case got and how high it reached. Three-tenths is organisational reach: how many of the 105 tracked organisations have a documented national presence in the country. One-fifth is conditions, from the Global Organized Crime Index 2025: how freely officials act for hidden principals and how little stops them. Where a country has no documented case the score is a best-judgement estimate of likelihood, and its popup is marked as one.

The second layer is the documented record: 422 cases in which a court, a parliamentary or official inquiry, a government designation, a regulator or the organisation itself established that it had members or agents inside a public institution. Each names the office reached and the forum that found it. Roberto Calvi is one: chairman of Banco Ambrosiano and a member of the P2 lodge, found hanging under Blackfriars Bridge in London in June 1982. Rome magistrates concluded in 2002 that he had been murdered; five people were tried for it and acquitted in 2007. Ambrosiano collapsed with about $1.3 billion missing, much of it lent to shell companies the Vatican Bank stood behind, and in 1984 the Vatican Bank paid $224 million to the creditors, citing "moral involvement" and admitting no liability.

The third layer is the organisations: 105 headquarters, 1,096 national branches and chapters, and 74 documented channels along which members, money or orders moved between them. A branch dot marks presence in a country, not proof of infiltration there. The organisations are not only secret societies: they cover every kind of international body counted in the Union of International Associations' Yearbook of International Organizations that has reached inside a government — lodges, religious orders, policy clubs, covert and state-run networks, foundations, intelligence fronts, and intergovernmental bodies such as Interpol and the WHO.

The fourth layer reads across all of these. The patterns panel below shows the arrangements that recur — the same people, banks and services appearing in different countries and decades — and each country box has a behind-the-scenes write-up that ends with what it means for someone without the time to piece it together.
